newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr snowed under by Japanese sales.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr snowed under by Japanese sales.

text.p: The Australian dollar took to the slopes Friday as the market was snowed under by Japanese investor sales for the second day in a row.

The currency had spent much of the day building a base around US$0.7650 after surviving a visit to 76 cents offshore, but support melted in minutes when a Japanese securities house dumped AUD/yen in size.

Dealers said local, European and U.S. investors seemed content to buy beneath 76 cents based on the view that domestic rates would not be cut anytime soon, but the weight of pressure would be all downhill while Tokyo was in such a selling mood.

By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was buried at US$0.7605/10 having skidded from an early US$0.7645/50. The action mirrored Thursday's gyrations which saw it bounce to US$0.7680 before collapsing to US$0.7610/15 by the close.
Analysts said the medium term direction would be set by which broke first, US$0.7585 support or US$0.7735 resistance with either likely to yield a move of at least a cent.

Pure proximity favoured the downside, although some felt the risk/reward ratio argued against going short since the main bear target of 75 cents was only a cent away, while the accepted potential for recovery stretched all the way to 80 cents.
Japanese investors did not seem to share those sentiments, however, and were looking to take profits on AUD/yen positions built up over more than a year of heavy yen/A$ samurai buying.

And those profits were very tempting as the weakness of the yen was keeping the local dollar strong at 94.39/49 yen after touching a 4-1/2 year high of 94.88 Thursday. This helped limit losses on the trade weighted index to 58.3 from 58.4.

Traders said the local market still thought the rationale for buying the dollar was quite strong after Thursday's unexpectedly robust wages data extinguished all talk of a domestic rate cut this month.
An easing was still possible at the Reserve Bank's March board meeting but analysts felt the odds had lengthened given that annual wages growth was sure to top 4.0 percent in Q1.
That was reflected in the March 90-day bank bill future which dived to 94.16 from a contract high of 94.41, implying a rate of 5.84 percent against the official rate of 6.0 percent.
Nevertheless, the easing bias remained and contrasted unfavourably, at least for Japanese investors, with the U.S. and U.K. where the next move in rates was likely to be upwards.
This discontent found its expression in a dwindling flow of yen/A$ dual currency samurai issues.
January saw just a single 30 billion yen issue but in 1996 an estimated 1.9 trillion yen of these bonds were launched, according to figures from Colonial State Bank.

Instead, there had been an explosion of yen/US$ samurais since the yield between the US$ and the A$ had narrowed sharply following 150 basis points of easing here last year and Japanese retail investors felt more comfortable investing in US$.
Forward rates also favoured the former as strong U.S. growth meant the Federal Reserve had a tightening bias.
The A$ had also been overtaken by sterling as a U.K. hike and talk of more rises pushed most bond yields above those here.
Accordingly, samurais with a sterling element had become popular with Japanese retail investors desperate for better returns after more than a year of record low rates at home.

The A$ was also dogged by concerns about what the Japanese would do with funds released by maturing samurais, although some of the amounts rumoured were well over the mark. Colonial said only one 10 billion yen issue matured in February -- on the 13th to be precise -- and one of 50 billion yen on March 6.
There were none then until October and the real flood would only come in 1998 and 1999.
